name: Basalt
long_description:
Basalt is building Constellations as a Service, self-flying satellite constellations tailored for private enterprise and the government without any prior aerospace experience needed! Powered by our Diamond AI, Basalt provides a seamless experience, enabling users to fly and stream data and images from their own dedicated satellite constellation onto their phones and laptops.  

Basalt received its seed investment as part of the Y Combinator W24 batch, and has since launched Spirit-EEL, the world's first AI-controlled satellite constellation.

founders.title: Founder/CEO
founders.founder_bio:
CEO & Co-Founder of Basalt    //    I was working at Caltech’s fusion lab when I was hired out of high school to work at MIT AeroAstro on their CubeSat mission.

Since then, I’ve spent stints at The Aerospace Corporation and SpaceX working on distributed space systems and the American moon landing. Most recently, I dropped out to build Basalt. My hobbies include hiking and buying infinite whiteboards.

launches.title: Basalt: Constellations as a Service
launches.body:
\- BASALT

# **Why we’re here.**

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=79293&key=user_uploads/1408579/7709c01c-68e0-4de2-a932-e5bf387f88a3)

It’s been an exciting year for space. Basalt saw this excitement years ago. Founded in 2023, our mission at Basalt is to develop fully autonomous satellite constellations to challenge the legacy of the space industry. 

By mass producing satellites in-house and outfitting the fleet with autonomous tasking capabilities, anyone can operate their own Earth Observation and Real Time Intelligence satellites, skipping years of specialized training and eliminating queues and rental costs typical in other space data platforms. We are bringing space to everyone.

# **Expensive Data, Unreliable Delivery.**

In the current market, customers pay huge amounts of money for inconsistent data streams. 

Why?

A single live-tasked, sub-meter resolution image can be priced as high as $10 per square kilometer, with inconsistent availability for rural regions and no assured delivery of images without cloud coverage. We’ve tried out these platforms at Basalt, and between hoping archival imagery exists, waiting a week for a usable image, and paying thousands of dollars to expedite a task, our engineer summed it up as “a massive pain in the ass”.

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=79293&key=user_uploads/1408579/dc49df8c-f0d9-4f2b-af96-0a043cc7a662)

Imagery outages for volatile locations are common. Legacy imagery providers are [subject to government blackouts](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/opinion/satellite-images-us-government.html). As a result, commercial markets are forced to treat space as a pricy experiment.

# **What’s on the Table Now.**

We’re not the first to realize that this is an issue, and dedicated satellite makers have seen early success. Our goal is to scale that business model.

An early player in the space data economy, ICEYE actually experienced customers struggling to scale up using space data, and is starting to [pivot towards selling dedicated satellites](https://satnews.com/2026/03/15/iceye-targets-e1-billion-revenue-threshold-as-defense-demand-drives-production-scaling/) outright. This is a great move on their part, but ICEYE only builds SAR satellites, which are very expensive, and mainly useful for defense customers.

A quick aside: SAR stands for synthetic aperture radar. It is [an impressive feat of engineering](https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/learn/earth-observation-data-basics/sar) that builds sensing capability that isn’t affected by cloud cover and day-night cycles.

Muon Space builds dedicated custom spacecraft, but their buses are too expensive for market adoption. While they have reshaped how spacecraft are built through their vertically integrated platform, high cost limits their customer base significantly. Muon customers also [do not have direct control over their systems](https://www.spacecapital.com/blogs/muon-space-rewriting-playbook-for-earth-intelligence), causing operational delay in these constellations. 

NanoAvionics sells satellite buses and individual components, and are a popular partner among companies that build their own satellites. The problem is obvious if you want your own dedicated satellite swarm but don’t have aerospace engineers in-house: buying the parts still leaves you to integrate, launch, and operate the spacecraft. 

This isn’t to say that these companies don’t serve their customers well. ICEYE, Muon Space, and NanoAvionics have paved the way for better access to space, but that access is still limited to governments and aerospace firms. 

Basalt was built on their advancements, and brings autonomous satellite constellations to a much wider market segment.

# **Basalt is selling the Falcon 9 of space systems.**

Falcon 9 rockets did not win on exotic, novel technology. Instead, SpaceX took simple, low efficiency engines and flew them at a cadence no one could dream of. SpaceX won because they costs down by multiple orders of magnitude, not because their technology was research-grade and unique.

Basalt is running this strategy on space systems and constellations.

Basalt constellations run on Lantern, our 16U satellite bus built to maximize capability per dollar.

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=79293&key=user_uploads/1408579/f5a0f6f4-7fbd-468c-9732-29723e433ed8)

So how do we keep costs down? Plenty of space startups are building bold, first-of-their-kind technology that could reshape what’s possible in orbit. We’re focusing on something else: driving down cost by stripping out complexity, without sacrificing reliability. The playbook for doing that is well proven:

* **One standard platform**. Sharing structures and avionics means we’re not paying for a new design for each mission.
* **Plug-and-play payloads.** Customers mix and match sensors to build the constellation they need, without paying for custom engineering. 
* **Design for manufacturing and assembly.** Fewer parts and simpler builds mean fewer labor hours per satellite.
* **Commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) electronics.** Proven commercial parts are reliable, ship faster, and cost a fraction of custom components.
* **In-house manufacturing.** Building key parts ourselves cuts supplier markups and keeps schedules in our control.
* **AI-driven operations.** Diamond AI, our homegrown autonomy platform. This allows any customer to own and directly control their satellites, no in-house aerospace experience required.

The result is a dedicated constellation that you own and control. We’re not claiming the state of the art at Basalt, but [neither did SpaceX](https://everydayastronaut.com/starbase-tour-and-interview-with-elon-musk/).

# **New Faces, Bigger Fleets.**

We joke at the office that owning a Basalt satellite is like paying a (_very_ luxury) car payment.

In reality, a Basalt satellite costs about the same as hiring an [aerospace engineer](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/architecture-and-engineering/aerospace-engineers.htm) and a [data scientist](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/math/data-scientists.htm), the two roles it effectively replaces. Basalt’s monthly payments start at $21,670 for one dedicated satellite in orbit (launch included). 

For enterprise businesses, it's a budget line they already have. [Sending an analyst into a warzone](https://www.citriniresearch.com/p/strait-of-hormuz-a-citrini-field) does work, especially when things are uncertain; but wouldn’t you just want to command your own satellite constellation to capture real-time images that your competitors won’t have access to? (Our team does admit that being deployed like this is pretty cool).

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=79293&key=user_uploads/1408579/d38ca726-f49c-497a-956e-038f2d4ccfcb)

For established customers, Basalt brings a scalable, proliferated capability through CaaS. For example, the US Space Force can field complex, tactical space systems at a scale and pace not seen before, without waiting for new super-heavy launch vehicles to mature. Scale also allows defense customers to field and test new sensors quickly, across many satellites at once.

# **The Plan: Alameda and Beyond.**

Basalt is moving into the historic shipyard of Alameda. We spent a few years in the SF Tenderloin, and while we will miss being in the city, we’re trading it for more room to build. Our new facility will reach a rate of up to 100 satellites per year by the end of 2028, serving customers in commercial risk markets and defense. This factory will support buildout of > $85M in planned customer constellations.

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=79293&key=user_uploads/1408579/5873cce6-7699-4d93-a62c-d7c947bbed44)

Building satellites here is part of Basalt's broader effort to rebuild American industrial capacity, right here in the Bay Area. 

Our first mission, Lux-1, will demonstrate the Lantern autonomous platform, and is manifested to launch in Q4 2027. But Lux-1 is a production demonstration, not a technology one. We’ll be building for customers alongside the demo rather than in series. 

On the commercial side, interest is coming from maritime monitoring, energy, risk analytics, insurance, and space data insights. Many of these companies already buy satellite data from commercial imagery providers, but CaaS is their first opportunity to bring their own data pipeline in-house.

On the government side, we’ve been engaging with government customers, teaming with defense primes, and applying for contracts across all agencies. We’ll be participating in Talisman Sabre in 2027, Australia’s largest military exercise, run with US Indo-Pacific Command (INDOPACOM) and more than 20 partner nations across the Indo-Pacific. Our team brings decades of experience from the military and intelligence community to bear.

Things are moving quickly at Basalt. We’re creating a new playing field in space, and we hope you’ll join us for the ride. 

### **Learn more.**

Check out our [website](https://basalt.space/)!

Interested in how we can help streamline your mission? Set up a [meeting](https://basalt.space/contact).
